title: The hospitals
hookLine: hospitals treat all who come, rich or poor, with wards and music (historians)

cards: A traveler falls ill far from home. No family nearby, no money, no one who knows his name. But historians describe, in the great cities of the Muslim world, a building where he could walk in the door.
Separate wards for different illnesses. Physicians on rounds, students behind them. A pharmacy.

Water running through the courtyard. And in some of these houses, the historians say, musicians played for the patients, and storytellers sat with those who could not sleep. Nobody asked first whether he could pay.
The building had a Persian name: bimaristan.

teach.h: BIMARISTAN: THE PLACE OF THE SICK.
teach.b: Bimaristan is usually explained as the place of the sick. The word came into Arabic from Persian, and in Cairo and Damascus, Baghdad and beyond, it named a hospital. Three things made these houses work.
Historians describe them as paid for by waqf, an endowment: a ruler or a wealthy donor set aside shops, farms or rents forever, and their income kept the hospital open.
Care was free because someone, long before, had given.

Second, the order inside: wards for fevers, for eye diseases, for surgery, for those whose minds were troubled. Physicians trained students at the bedside, and records were kept. Third, the door: care for all who come.
Men and women, rich and poor, locals and strangers. Muslims trace that door back to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.

teach.h: VISIT THE SICK. SEEK THE CURE.
teach.b: In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, he tells his followers to feed the hungry, visit the sick, and free the captive. In another, he says that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure.
Visiting the sick was already a teaching of the Prophet.
Looking for the cure was an act of hope. And the Qur'an, in a passage addressed to the Children of Israel, says that whoever saves one life, it is as if he had saved all humanity.
Some have seen that verse put into stone in a hospital that turns no one away. Tomorrow, one of the physicians who walked those wards.

how: Visiting the sick is a practice Muslims trace to the Prophet's teaching, and in Muslim history hospitals were often funded as waqf, a charitable endowment, so they could treat people who could not pay.

games.q: you've built a hospital and need it to stay open long after you die. what do you do?
o: charge every patient at the door.
set aside shops and farms as an endowment.
ask the next ruler to pay, and hope.
games.why: a waqf: income from endowed property kept the doors open and the care free.

practice: Bring to mind one hospital you know and picture its door and the people walking through it today, some frightened, some alone.
Breathe for them, and choose one small way to give: a little to a clinic that treats people who can't pay, or a visit to someone who is sick.
If you pray, you can pray for the patients and the people caring for them; if not, just hold them in mind.
